claim: Larval zebrafish that are exposed repeatedly to dark looming stimuli will quickly habituate to these aversive signals and cease to respond with their stereotypical escape swims.
source: Larval zebrafish that are exposed repeatedly to dark looming stimuli will quickly habituate to these aversive signals and cease to respond with their stereotypical escape swims.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by behavioral experiments showing declining response probability with repeated stimulation.

claim: A dark looming stimulus can be separated into two independent components: one characterized by spatial expansion with maintained luminance, and one representing overall dimming without motion energy.
source: A dark looming stimulus can be separated into two independent components: one that is characterized by an overall spatial expansion, where overall luminance is maintained at the same level, and a second, that represents an overall dimming within the whole visual field in the absence of any motion energy.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the use of checkerboard stimuli (expansion without dimming) and dimming stimuli (dimming without expansion) in the experiments.

claim: There exist two separate neural pathways for processing looming stimuli: a looming channel responding to expanding edges and a dimming-specific channel.
source: Concurrent brain wide imaging experiments then permitted the construction of circuit models that suggest the existence of two separate neural pathways. The first is a looming channel which responds specifically to expanding edges presented to the contralateral eye and relays that information to the brain stem escape network to generate directed escapes. The second is a dimming-specific channel that could be either monocular or binocularly responsive, and that appears to specifically inhibit escape response when activated.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data showing distinct functional clusters of neurons (LS and DS) with different response properties and anatomical distributions.

claim: The dimming-specific channel is primarily responsible for the incremental silencing of successive dark looming-evoked escapes.
source: We propose that this second channel is under strong contextual modulation and that it is primarily responsible for the incremental silencing of successive dark looming-evoked escapes.
evidence: This is supported by pre-habituation experiments showing that dimming stimuli alone can habituate responses to dark looming.

claim: Habituation is the simplest form of learning and is ubiquitous across the animal kingdom.
source: Habituation or reduced responsiveness to repeated stimulation is the simplest form of learning and is ubiquitous across the animal kingdom (Rankin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: The gill withdrawal reflex in Aplysia habituates through the local network of neurons in the abdominal ganglion.
source: One famous example is the habituation of the gill withdrawal reflex to a brief touch stimulus through the local network of neurons in the abdominal ganglion in Aplysia (Glanzman, 2009; Kandel, 2001; Rankin et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to established research on Aplysia.

claim: Escape responses to quick tap stimuli in larval zebrafish habituate through the Mauthner cell circuitry in the hindbrain.
source: another well-studied phenomenon is the habituation of escape responses to quick tap stimuli in larval zebrafish through the Mauthner cell circuitry in the hindbrain (Marsden and Granato, 2015; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies on zebrafish escape habituation.

claim: Less is known about neural mechanisms and computational algorithms that underlie habituation of behaviors executed at longer time scales with slowly varying sensory stimuli.
source: Less is known about neural mechanisms and computational algorithms that underlie habituation of behaviors that get executed at distinctly longer time scales, and where the sensory stimuli vary more slowly in time.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field based on literature review.

claim: Processing of looming stimuli involves extracting behaviorally relevant kinematic variables such as angular size, speed, and time remaining to collision based on spatio-temporal structure of sensory input.
source: Objects approaching on a collision course, such as a looming predator, are good examples of such stimuli the processing of which often involves extracting behaviorally relevant kinematic variables such as angular size, speed, and time remaining to collision based on the spatio-temporal structure of the sensory input (Fotowat and Gabbiani, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on looming stimulus processing.

claim: In locusts, looming computation is carried out across layers of the optic lobes through three restricted dendritic fields of the Lobula Giant Movement Detectors (LGMD).
source: In invertebrates such as locusts this computation is carried out across layers of the optic lobes and especially through three restricted dendritic fields of a pair of identified neurons, the Lobula Giant Movement Detectors (LGMD) (Gabbiani et al., 1999; Peron et al., 2009; Jones and Gabbiani, 2010; Gabbiani et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research on locust LGMD neurons.

claim: Distinct features of time-varying firing in LGMD neurons are extracted by downstream motor networks to drive execution of multi-stage escape behavior.
source: Distinct features of the time-varying firing in these neurons are in turn extracted by the downstream motor networks to drive the execution of a multi-stage escape behavior (Fotowat et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on LGMD-motor network interactions.

claim: In fish, neurons tuned to looming stimuli are found in the optic tectum and perform computations similar to LGMD neurons but use a more distributed network.
source: In vertebrates such as fish, neurons tuned to looming stimuli are found in the optic tectum and are thought to perform computations similar to those carried out by the LGMD neurons, but these vertebrate animals tend to use a more distributed network of neurons (Dunn et al., 2016; Temizer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on zebrafish looming-responsive neurons.

claim: Information from the visual system is relayed to downstream motor networks which can trigger distinct types of escapes in a context-dependent manner.
source: Information is then relayed from the visual system to the downstream motor networks which can trigger distinct types of escapes in a context-dependent manner (Bhattacharyya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on context-dependent escape behaviors.

claim: The two Mauthner cells encode the course of stimulus approach in their time-varying subthreshold membrane potential and trigger a fast escape once a voltage threshold is crossed.
source: Specifically, the two Mauthner cells, a pair of identified giant neurons in the hindbrain, further encode the course of stimulus approach in their time-varying subthreshold membrane potential, and will trigger a fast escape once a voltage threshold is crossed (Preuss et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on Mauthner cell physiology.

claim: Escaping too early is undesirable as it gives time for a predator to revise its attack strategy or might not be necessary if the detected object is not an attacking predator.
source: Escaping too early or prematurely is undesirable as it will give enough time for a predator to revise its attack strategy, or it might not be necessary if the detected approaching object is in fact not an attacking predator.
evidence: This is based on logical inference about predator-prey interactions.

claim: Depending on the speed of the approaching predator and other environmental cues, it might be more advantageous to freeze than to escape or vice versa.
source: For example, depending on the speed of the approaching predator and other environmental cues, it might be more advantageous to freeze than to escape or vice versa (Bhattacharyya et al., 2017; Evans et al., 2019; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on context-dependent defensive behaviors.

claim: Habituation to looming stimuli has been reported in various animal species, and the speed of habituation depends on behavioral context.
source: In fact, habituation to looming stimuli has been reported in various animal species, and the speed of habituation itself is known to depend on the behavioral context (Hayes and Saiff, 1967; Matheson et al., 2004; Oliva et al., 2007; Mancienne et al., 2021; Marquez-Legorreta et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies across different species.

claim: In larval zebrafish, neurons specifically tuned to looming are largely represented in the optic tectum, specifically within the Stratum periventriculare.
source: In larval zebrafish, neurons that are specifically tuned to looming, are largely represented in the optic tectum, specifically within the Stratum periventriculare (Dunn et al., 2016; Temizer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Neurons that respond to sudden or gradual changes in luminance are present in retinal ganglion cell arborization fields AF6 and AF8, as well as the optic tectum, pretectum, and thalamus.
source: Neurons that respond to sudden or gradual changes in luminance (dimming and dark flash stimuli, respectively) are present at the level of the retinal ganglion cell arborization fields AF6 and AF8, as well as the optic tectum, pretectum, and thalamus (Temizer et al., 2015; Heap et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: The dimming aspect of a dark looming stimulus is necessary for driving escapes, as bright expanding disks rarely evoke escape, however dimming alone is generally not sufficient.
source: It was found that the dimming aspect of a dark looming stimulus is necessary for driving escapes, as bright expanding disks rarely evoke escape, however, dimming alone is generally not sufficient (Temizer et al., 2015; Mancienne et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Dark flash responsive dopaminergic neurons in the caudal hypothalamus inhibit downstream escape motor networks and help differentiate threatening from non-threatening stimuli.
source: In fact, Yao et al., 2016 have identified dark flash (i.e., fast dimming) responsive dopaminergic neurons in the caudal hypothalamus that inhibit downstream escape motor networks, and are thought to help differentiate a threatening (looming) from a non-threatening (dark flash/dimming) stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific prior study.

claim: Head-embedded tail-free fish habituate faster than freely swimming fish.
source: Second, tethered fish tend to habituate faster than those freely swimming (personal observation, also see Ahrens et al., 2012)
evidence: This is based on personal observation and citation to prior work.

claim: A subpopulation of dimming-sensitive potentiating neurons actively suppresses responses of looming-sensitive neurons that relay information to elicit escapes in a habituating larva.
source: Specifically, we propose that a subpopulation of dimming-sensitive (DS) potentiating neurons actively suppresses responses of the looming-sensitive (LS) neurons that relay critical information to elicit escapes in the brain of a habituating larva.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on calcium imaging data showing DSPOT neurons and their effects on LS neurons.

claim: There is a separate pathway that relies exclusively on the expanding motion aspect and can independently contribute to the habituation process.
source: We also find evidence for a separate pathway that relies exclusively on the expanding motion aspect, and that can independently contribute to the habituation process.
evidence: This is based on behavioral data showing habituation to checkerboard stimuli.

claim: Animals executed a tail flick during the first presentation of a looming stimulus with a probability of approximately 60%.
source: Using this configuration, we found that animals executed a tail flick during the first presentation of a looming stimulus in a stochastic manner with a probability of ~60%.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from behavioral experiments.

claim: The baseline rate of spontaneous tail flicks was approximately 0.026 Hz on average and did not change significantly throughout the experiment.
source: Measuring the rate of spontaneous tail flicks in the absence of stimulation confirmed a baseline rate of approximately 0.026 Hz on average, which did not change significantly throughout the experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, b).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Response probability and response amplitude decreased with stimulus repetition in an ISI-dependent manner, with longer ISI resulting in slower rate of reduction.
source: We observed that response probability, as well as response amplitude, decreased with stimulus repetition in an ISI-dependent manner. The longer the ISI, the slower the rate of reduction with repetition (red curves, Figure 1b, d, e, left and right panels correspond to ISI = 180 and 10 s, respectively).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The escape response largely recovered when the stimulus was switched to the contralateral eye, although a slight carry over of habituation was observed.
source: Interestingly, the escape response largely recovered when the stimulus was switched to the contralateral eye, although a slight carry over of habituation was observed.
evidence: This is shown in behavioral data in Figure 1d, e.

claim: The timing of escape was tightly coupled to the stimulus onset across trials.
source: As expected, we find that the timing of escape was tightly coupled to the stimulus onset across trials (Figure 1f)
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Responses were largely biased to the direction away from the stimulated eye.
source: and that the responses were largely biased to the direction away from the stimulated eye (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is shown in behavioral data in Figure 1g.

claim: Both dark looming and checkerboard stimuli were effective in triggering escapes, while dimming stimuli were not.
source: We found that both dark looming and checkerboard stimuli were effective in triggering escapes, while the dimming stimuli were not (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments comparing different stimulus types shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The amplitude and timing of escape were similar for dark looming and checkerboard looming stimuli.
source: The amplitude and timing of escape were similar for dark looming and checkerboard looming stimuli (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Pre-habituation with dimming was very effective in reducing responses to the dark looming stimulus, while pre-habituation with checkerboards had little effect.
source: Interestingly, we found that pre-habituation with dimming was very effective in reducing responses to the dark looming stimulus, while pre-habituation with checkerboards, that lacked the dimming aspect, had little effect.
evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Fish pre-exposed to five dimming stimuli showed no response to subsequent presentation of five dark looming stimuli.
source: The first set, shown on the top panel, was pre-exposed to five dimming stimuli (blue line), and, remarkably, showed no response to subsequent presentation of five dark looming stimuli (red line).
evidence: This is shown in behavioral data in Figure 2c, top panel.

claim: Fish pre-exposed and habituated completely to 10 checkerboard stimuli responded strongly to subsequent presentation of dark looming stimuli.
source: The second set (Figure 2c, bottom panel), on the other hand, was pre-exposed – and habituated completely – to 10 checkerboard stimuli (purple), and yet responded strongly to subsequent presentation of dark looming stimuli (red line).
evidence: This is shown in behavioral data in Figure 2c, bottom panel.

claim: All responsive neurons could be divided into 16 clusters based on a 4-digit binary code corresponding to response strength to each of four stimulus types.
source: Using this technique, we could divide all responsive neurons into 16 clusters (4-digit binary code corresponding to response strength to each of the four stimulus types).
evidence: This is the result of clustering analysis on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Many neurons responded strongly to dimming or brightening stimuli (clusters 12 and 2, respectively).
source: We found that many neurons responded strongly to dimming or brightening stimuli (clusters 12 and 2, respectively)
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: The next most abundant cell type consisted of neurons sensitive specifically to the looming stimulus (cluster 5), responding robustly to both dark looming and checkerboard stimuli but not to dimming or brightening.
source: but that the next most abundant cell type consisted of neurons that were sensitive specifically to the looming stimulus (cluster 5), that is cells that robustly responded to both dark looming and checkerboard stimuli, but not to dimming or brightening.
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: DS neurons respond to dark looming and dimming, and to the sudden transition from light to dark at the end of brightening stimuli.
source: DS neurons respond to dark looming and dimming, and, as expected, to the sudden transition from light to dark at the end of brightening stimuli.
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data in Figure 3b.

claim: LS neurons respond to both dark looming and checkerboard looming, but not to dimming or brightening stimuli.
source: LS neurons, on the other hand, respond to both dark looming and checkerboard looming, but not to dimming or brightening stimuli.
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data in Figure 3b.

claim: The average responses to all stimuli tended to decline with stimulus repetition, although this decline was faster for the LS cluster.
source: The average responses to all stimuli tended to decline with stimulus repetition, although this decline was faster for the LS cluster.
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data in Figure 3b.

claim: The peak activity of LS neurons occurred significantly earlier than that of DS neurons.
source: Notably, the peak activity of LS neurons occurred significantly earlier than that of DS neurons (Figure 3b, inset).
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data in Figure 3b inset.

claim: Neurons in the DS cluster were present in both brain hemispheres with a hemispheric index of 0.02.
source: Interestingly, we found that neurons in the DS cluster were present in both brain hemispheres (Figure 3c, blue dots, hemispheric index [HI] = 0.02, with the HI of zero corresponding to equal presence in the left and right hemispheres, see Methods)
evidence: This is shown in anatomical mapping data in Figure 3c.

claim: Neurons in the LS cluster were largely localized in the hemisphere contralateral to the stimulated eye with a hemispheric index of -0.86.
source: whereas neurons in the LS cluster were largely localized in the hemisphere contralateral to the stimulated eye (HI = −0.86, with −1 corresponding to the exclusive presence in the contralateral hemisphere).
evidence: This is shown in anatomical mapping data in Figure 3c.

claim: LS neurons are most abundant in tegmentum, tectum (stratum periventriculare), and hindbrain networks.
source: Consistent with previous studies we find that LS neurons are most abundant in tegmentum, tectum (stratum periventriculare), and hindbrain networks
evidence: This is shown in anatomical mapping data in Figure 3d, e and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: DS clusters dominate the pretectum, thalamus, and neuropil regions.
source: whereas the DS clusters dominate the pretectum, thalamus, and neuropil regions.
evidence: This is shown in anatomical mapping data in Figure 3d, e.

claim: DS neurons were more abundant than LS neurons in forebrain regions such as thalamus, pallium, and habenula.
source: Furthermore, we find that DS neurons were more abundant than LS neurons in forebrain regions such as thalamus, pallium, and habenula.
evidence: This is shown in anatomical mapping data in Figure 3d.

claim: Inhibitory neurons were found to cluster with little discrimination across all regions and response types in a salt and pepper fashion.
source: Finally, inhibitory neurons were found to cluster with little discrimination across all regions and response types in a salt and pepper fashion (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is shown in anatomical mapping data in Figure 3f.

claim: The majority (55%) of neurons decreased their responses with negative time constants and were termed 'depressing'.
source: Based on the distribution of the time constants, we found that the majority (55%) of neurons decreased their responses and were best fit with negative time constants (Figure 3g, green area, see Methods). This cluster was termed 'depressing'.
evidence: This is based on exponential fitting analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: A smaller percentage of cells (18%) displayed an increase in response amplitude with stimulus repetition with positive time constants and were termed 'potentiating'.
source: A smaller percentage of cells (18%) displayed an increase in response amplitude with stimulus repetition (Figure 3g, positive time constants, pink area), and was termed 'potentiating'.
evidence: This is based on exponential fitting analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: 27% of cells did not consistently change their response amplitude over repeated stimulation and were called 'stable'.
source: Finally, 27% of cells did not consistently change their response amplitude over repeated stimulation, and we call them 'stable'.
evidence: This is based on exponential fitting analysis of calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The great majority of LS neurons belong to the depressing group and their potentiating fraction was much smaller.
source: When we applied this classification to the LS and DS clusters, we found that the great majority of LS neurons belong to the depressing group (Figure 3h, top panel, Figure 3i, green segments), and that their potentiating fraction was much smaller (Figure 3h, bottom panel, Figure 3i, maroon segments).
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data analysis in Figure 3h, i.

claim: The DS cluster contained a prominent subcluster of potentiating cells (DSPOT).
source: The DS cluster on the other hand contained a prominent subcluster of potentiating cells (DSPOT, Figure 3j, k).
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data analysis in Figure 3j, k.

claim: DSPOT neurons present a significant portion of neurons in a large fraction of brain regions including habenula and pallium which are implicated in adaptive and dynamic control of behavior.
source: Interestingly, Figure 3k shows that DSPOT neurons (maroon segments) present a significant portion of neurons in a large fraction of the brain regions we recorded from, including areas such as the habenula and the palium which are implicated in the adaptive and dynamic control of behavior.
evidence: This is shown in anatomical distribution data in Figure 3k and draws on established knowledge about these brain regions.

claim: The DSPOT cluster contained more than 25% neurons with a GABAergic label, whereas the fraction of GABAergic neurons in the LS and declining DS clusters was 10% or less.
source: Consistent with the proposed model, we find that the DSPOT cluster contained more than 25% neurons with a GABAergic label, whereas the fraction of GABAergic neurons in the LS and declining DS clusters was 10% or less (Figure 3i, k, insets).
evidence: This is shown in the analysis of GABAergic labeling in Figure 3i, k insets.

claim: Covert potentiation of the dimming pathway led to a significantly reduced response size in LS neurons when compared to the largely recovered response size after a 10-min waiting period.
source: We find that such 'covert' potentiation of the dimming pathway led to a significantly reduced response size in LS neurons when compared to the largely – but not completely – recovered response size after a 10-min waiting period (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: LS neurons are similarly silent during the dimming stimulation period as they are during the waiting period.
source: Importantly, LS neurons are similarly silent during the dimming stimulation period, as they are during the waiting period (Figure 4b, c).
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data in Figure 4b, c.

claim: LS neurons responded mainly to stimuli presented to the contralateral eye with hemispheric indices of -0.89 and -0.94 for right and left eye stimulation, respectively.
source: We found that, as predicted, LS neurons responded mainly to stimuli presented to the contralateral eye (Figure 5a, HI = −0.89 and −0.94 for right and left eye stimulation, respectively, see Methods)
evidence: This is shown in binocular stimulation experiments in Figure 5a.

claim: DS neurons come in two classes: one class consists of monocular cells largely located on the contralateral side, and a second class consists of binocular neurons evenly distributed across hemispheres.
source: whereas DS neurons come in two classes: one class consists of monocular cells which are largely located on the contralateral side (Figure 5b, HI = −0.52 and −0.47 for right and left eye stimulation, respectively), and a second class that consists of binocular neurons which are evenly distributed across hemispheres (Figure 5c, HI = −0.04, see Methods).
evidence: This is shown in binocular stimulation experiments in Figure 5b, c.

claim: In both the binocular and monocular populations of DS neurons, about one-third of the individuals belong to the potentiating class.
source: Figure 6a shows that in both the binocular and the monocular populations of DS neurons, about one-third of the individuals belong to the potentiating class.
evidence: This is shown in analysis of DS neuron subclusters in Figure 6a.

claim: The general lack of transfer in behavioral habituation between the two eyes argues that DSPOT neurons exert their inhibitory influence in an eye-specific manner.
source: The general lack of transfer in behavioral habituation between the two eyes (Figure 1d and e) argues that DSPOT neurons exert their inhibitory influence in an eye-specific manner which suggests that the monocular DSPOT neurons are the critical components for this feature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of behavioral and anatomical data.

claim: The residual transfer in habituation observed in behavioral experiments predicts the existence of binocular DSPOT neurons that continue their trend of potentiation when the stimulus is switched across eyes.
source: The residual transfer in habituation that we observe in behavioral experiments predicts the existence of binocular DSPOT neurons that continue their trend of potentiation when the stimulus is switched across eyes (Figure 6c, top panel).
evidence: This is an inference based on behavioral data and confirmed by calcium imaging data in Figure 6c.

claim: The number of binocular DSPOT neurons (n = 46) is smaller than the total number of monocular DSPOT cells (n = 118).
source: Note that the number of these cells (n = 46) is smaller than the total number of monocular DSPOT cells (n = 118).
evidence: This is a direct count from the calcium imaging data.

claim: A small number of binocular resetting DSPOT neurons (n = 5) might contribute to the monocular specificity of the habituation process.
source: We also found a small number of binocular resetting DSPOT neurons (Figure 6c, bottom panel, n = 5) who might contribute to the monocular specificity of the habituation process.
evidence: This is shown in calcium imaging data in Figure 6c and represents a speculative interpretation.

claim: Tethered larvae habituate to repeated stimulation with dark looming stimuli presented from the side to one eye in an ISI-dependent manner, consistent with studies in freely swimming larvae.
source: Consistent with studies in freely swimming larvae (Mancienne et al., 2021; Marquez-Legorreta et al., 2022) we found that the tethered larvae habituate to repeated stimulation with dark looming stimuli presented from the side to one eye, in an ISI-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data and citations to prior studies.

claim: The 'dark looming' pathway is distinguished from the 'checkerboard' pathway by being selective for homogeneous expansion features that are absent in the expanding 'patchy' checkerboard.
source: That is, we suggest that the 'dark looming' pathway is distinguished from this 'checkerboard' pathway by being selective for homogeneous expansion features that are absent in the expanding 'patchy' checkerboard.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential habituation patterns observed with different stimulus types.

claim: In a previous study where looming stimuli were presented from below to freely swimming animals, pre-exposure to dimming did not significantly affect the response to subsequent dark looming.
source: Our results differ from reports from a previous study where looming stimuli were presented from below, rather than from the side as in our experiments, and where animals were freely swimming and not tethered. In this study, pre-exposure to dimming did not seem to significantly affect the response to subsequent dark looming (Mancienne et al., 2021)
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Binocular DS neurons were recently reported in the larval zebrafish tectum where the pathway of interhemispheric transfer was shown to be located in the Torus Longitudinalis.
source: Such binocular DS neurons were recently also reported in the larval zebrafish tectum (Tesmer et al., 2022) where the pathway of interhemispheric transfer was shown to be located in the Torus Longitudinalis, which itself receives input from the tectum (DeMarco et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies on binocular neurons and interhemispheric pathways.

claim: Axons of both looming and dimming responsive neurons project to hindbrain motor regions.
source: This hypothesis is supported by previous studies that have shown that axons of both looming and dimming responsive neurons project to hindbrain motor regions (Helmbrecht et al., 2018; Zottoli et al., 1987; Sato et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: A group of dark flash responding dopaminergic neurons in the caudal hypothalamus drives inhibition of the Mauthner cells via hindbrain glycinergic interneurons.
source: Interestingly, a group of dark flash responding dopaminergic neurons was identified in the caudal hypothalamus and was shown to drive inhibition of the Mauthner cells via hindbrain glycinergic interneurons (Yao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Glycinergic inhibition is thought to play a critical role in modulating responsiveness of hindbrain escape circuitry in general.
source: Indeed, glycinergic inhibition is thought to play a critical role in modulating responsiveness of hindbrain escape circuitry in general (Koyama et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Glycinergic inhibition has been shown to be specifically implicated in dampening responsiveness of Mauthner cells during habituation of acoustic startle response.
source: and it has been shown to be specifically implicated in dampening responsiveness of Mauthner cells during habituation of acoustic startle response (Marsden and Granato, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on acoustic startle habituation.

claim: All retinofugal projections in the zebrafish are exclusively contralateral.
source: The fact that all retinofugal projections in the zebrafish are exclusively contralateral indicates that LS neurons must be largely monocular.
evidence: This is based on established anatomical knowledge of zebrafish visual system.

claim: Looming stimuli with an absolute size-to-speed ratio (l/|v|) of 240 ms elicited escapes that occurred on average 1.3 s (SD = 0.5 s) before the expected collision time.
source: Looming stimuli, with an absolute size-to-speed ratio (l/|v|) of 240 ms (see Methods), elicited escapes that occurred on average 1.3 s (SD = 0.5 s) before the expected collision time (Figure 1b, c, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c, negative = before collision)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from behavioral experiments.

claim: Escapes displayed varying degrees of vigor, defined as the peak tail deflection amplitude.
source: and these escapes displayed varying degrees of vigor, defined as the peak tail deflection amplitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is shown in behavioral data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Escapes were generally directed away from the side of stimulus presentation with a probability of 0.76.
source: Further, escapes were generally directed away from the side of stimulus presentation, as expected (negative amplitude = away; probability of tail flick away from the stimulus = 0.76, Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from behavioral experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Looming-evoked responses could be classified into three groups: (1) a large tail bend + a counter bend, (2) a single large tail bend, or (3) one or more small tail flicks.
source: Using data from these experiments, we could classify looming-evoked responses into three groups: (1) a large tail bend + a counter bend, (2) a single large tail bend, or (3) one or more small tail flicks (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–e) (see Methods).
evidence: This is based on clustering analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The beating of the fins stopped (they were 'tucked-in') before large tail flicks, consistent with prior studies.
source: Consistent with prior studies (McClenahan et al., 2012), we found that the beating of the fins stopped that is they were 'tucked-in' before large tail flicks (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b, right column and Figure 1—figure supplement 2f).
evidence: This is shown in behavioral data and is consistent with prior work.

claim: In some trials, the fins stopped beating even in the absence of a tail flick, which are likely a form of freezing response.
source: We further observed that in some trials, the fins stopped beating even in the absence of a tail flick (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a, c, iv). Such behaviors are likely a form of freezing response.
evidence: This is an observation from behavioral data with an interpretation.

claim: The timing of fin tuck in freeze or escape trials did not show a significant difference, indicating that freezing might be a 'halted' escape response.
source: Interestingly, the timing of fin tuck in freeze or escape trials did not show a significant difference (Figure 1—figure supplement 2f), indicating that freezing might be a 'halted' escape response.
evidence: This is based on behavioral measurements with an interpretation.

claim: The spontaneous rate of tail flicks varied across experiments/animals and had a mean (SD) of 0.0266 (0.0730) Hz.
source: The spontaneous rate varied across experiments/animals and had a mean (SD) of 0.0266 (0.0730) Hz.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from behavioral experiments.

claim: Images were acquired at 1 Hz at 1024 × 1034 pixels resolution during calcium imaging experiments.
source: Images were acquired at 1 Hz at 1024 × 1034 pixels resolution.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Only one plane was imaged per fish in order to characterize the response dynamics of cells from the first encounter to a given stimulus.
source: Only one plane was imaged per fish in order to characterize the response dynamics of cells from the first encounter to a given stimulus.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: A cell was considered GABAergic if the red label covered more than 70% of its ROI.
source: A cell was considered GABAergic if the red label covered more than 70% of its ROI.

claim: The center Gaussian mean for the time constant distribution was -3.76 × 10^-5 (95% confidence interval -3.87 × 10^-5, -3.66 × 10^-5) and was significantly smaller than zero.
